---
title: "Performance Benchmark"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  echo = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  fig.align = "center"
)
library(ggplot2)

results <- read.csv("benchmark-results.csv")
environment_log <- readLines("benchmark-environment.log")

device_names <- c(png = "PNG", pdf = "PDF")

# The value of `column` in the one result row matching all of `...`.
result <- function(..., column = "median_ms") {
  conditions <- list(...)
  rows <- Reduce(
    `&`,
    Map(
      function(name, value) results[[name]] %in% value,
      names(conditions),
      conditions
    )
  )
  value <- results[[column]][rows]
  stopifnot(length(value) == 1)
  value
}

# Milliseconds as text: "85 ms", or seconds from one second up.
ms <- function(x) {
  ifelse(x >= 1000, sprintf("%.2f s", x / 1000), sprintf("%.0f ms", x))
}
ms2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f ms", x)
times <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)

per_label <- function(method, device, n = max_rows) {
  result(
    section = "geom",
    method = method,
    device = device,
    n = n,
    column = "per_label_ms"
  )
}

# A table with one row per `rows` value and one column per device.
by_device <- function(data, rows, value = "median_ms", format = ms) {
  table <- data.frame(unique(data[rows]), check.names = FALSE)
  for (device in names(device_names)) {
    keys <- do.call(paste, data[data$device == device, rows, drop = FALSE])
    values <- data[[value]][data$device == device]
    table[[device_names[[device]]]] <- format(values[match(
      do.call(paste, table[rows]),
      keys
    )])
  }
  table
}

max_rows <- max(results$n[results$section == "geom"])
```

This article measures how long plots with `ggtypst` labels take to draw, compared with the
same plots labeled by `ggplot2` itself (`geom_text()`, `element_text()`) and by
[`ggtext`](https://wilkelab.org/ggtext/). It helps you estimate the cost in your own work and
choose the right tool.

Every measurement is a whole plot: from building the `ggplot` object to the file written by
`ggsave()`, as PNG (drawn by `ragg`) and as PDF (drawn by `pdf()`). Every label is different,
in every plot and in every run, as in real data. The results come from
`tools/benchmark.R` (see [Reproducing the benchmark](#reproducing-the-benchmark)) on the machine
described in [Test environment](#test-environment).

## Summary

```{r}
#| label: summary-numbers
png_typst <- per_label("geom_typst", "png")
png_ggtext <- per_label("geom_richtext", "png")
png_text <- per_label("geom_text", "png")
pdf_typst <- per_label("geom_typst", "pdf")
pdf_ggtext <- per_label("geom_richtext", "pdf")
pdf_text <- per_label("geom_text", "pdf")
math_png <- per_label("geom_math_typst", "png")
math_pdf <- per_label("geom_math_typst", "pdf")
mitex_png <- per_label("geom_math_mitex", "png")
plotmath_png <- per_label("geom_text(parse = TRUE)", "png")

first_plot <- function(package, device) {
  result(
    section = "cold start",
    package = package,
    device = device,
    measure = "first plot"
  )
}
load_time <- function(package, device = "png") {
  result(
    section = "cold start",
    package = package,
    device = device,
    measure = "load"
  )
}
```

- **Label layers.** With `r max_rows` labels, each `geom_typst()` label adds about
  **`r ms2(png_typst)`** to a PNG and **`r ms2(pdf_typst)`** to a PDF. That is
  `r times(png_ggtext / png_typst)` times faster than `ggtext::geom_richtext()` for PNG
  (`r ms2(png_ggtext)` per label) and `r times(pdf_ggtext / pdf_typst)` times faster for PDF
  (`r ms2(pdf_ggtext)`). Plain `geom_text()`, which cannot style text, remains far cheaper
  (`r ms2(png_text)` and `r ms2(pdf_text)` per label).
- **Math.** A formula costs a little more than styled text (`r ms2(math_png)` per label for
  PNG), and LaTeX math through MiTeX costs about the same as Typst math (`r ms2(mitex_png)`).
  `ggplot2`'s plotmath (`geom_text(parse = TRUE)`) is faster (`r ms2(plotmath_png)`) but much
  more limited.
- **A few labels** (titles, a handful of annotations) add only a few milliseconds to a plot
  that already takes `r ms(result(section = "geom", method = "geom_point only", device = "png", n = 1))`
  to save as PNG.
- **Each label costs more in PDF than in PNG** with `ggtypst`, because `pdf()` only refers to
  fonts by name: `ggtypst` draws its text there as outlines so it looks the same everywhere. See
  `?ggtypst-options` for devices that draw native glyphs.
- **Theme text** such as titles, legends, and facet strips costs about the same as with
  `ggtext`; many tick labels cost more (see [Theme elements](#theme-elements)).
- **The first plot of a session** takes about
  `r ms(first_plot("ggtypst", "png") - first_plot("ggplot2", "png"))` longer than with plain
  `ggplot2`, while `ggtypst` loads its fonts and Typst. Loading the package itself costs little.

## Label layers

The plots have one point per row and label each point. Styled text is bold and italic, such as
`*Bold 12* _italic_ text` in `geom_typst()` and `<b>Bold 12</b> <i>italic</i> text` in
`ggtext::geom_richtext()` (with its box, padding and margin turned off); `geom_text()` draws the
same words without styling. Formulas are equivalent in Typst math, LaTeX (MiTeX), and plotmath,
such as `x_12^2 + alpha / (beta + 12)`.

```{r}
#| label: geom-plot
#| fig.alt: >
#|   Line charts of the time to build and save a plot against the number of labels, from 1 to
#|   1000, on log scales. Panels show styled text and math labels as PNG and as PDF.
geom <- results[results$section == "geom", ]
geom$content <- ifelse(geom$content == "math", "Math", "Styled text")
base <- geom[geom$method == "geom_point only", ]
geom <- geom[geom$method != "geom_point only", ]
geom <- rbind(
  geom,
  transform(base, content = "Styled text"),
  transform(base, content = "Math")
)
geom$device <- factor(device_names[geom$device], levels = device_names)
geom$content <- factor(geom$content, levels = c("Styled text", "Math"))
tools <- c(
  "geom_point only" = "No labels",
  "geom_text" = "ggplot2: geom_text()",
  "geom_text(parse = TRUE)" = "ggplot2: geom_text()",
  "geom_richtext" = "ggtext: geom_richtext()",
  "geom_typst" = "ggtypst",
  "geom_math_typst" = "ggtypst",
  "geom_math_mitex" = "ggtypst: MiTeX"
)
geom$tool <- factor(tools[geom$method], levels = unique(tools))

ggplot(geom, aes(n, median_ms / 1000, colour = tool)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = unique(geom$n)) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "No labels" = "grey60",
      "ggplot2: geom_text()" = "#264653",
      "ggtext: geom_richtext()" = "#e76f51",
      "ggtypst" = "#40A2B4",
      "ggtypst: MiTeX" = "#e9c46a"
    )
  ) +
  facet_grid(content ~ device) +
  labs(
    x = "Labels",
    y = "Time to build and save the plot (s)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The time grows linearly with the number of labels. The table gives the time each label adds:
the median time of the plot minus the same plot without labels, divided by the number of
labels.

```{r}
#| label: geom-table
per_row <- results[
  results$section == "geom" &
    results$method != "geom_point only" &
    results$n %in% c(10, 100, max_rows),
]
per_row$Labels <- per_row$n
per_row$Content <- ifelse(per_row$content == "math", "Math", "Styled text")
per_row$Function <- per_row$method
table <- by_device(
  per_row,
  c("Content", "Function", "Labels"),
  value = "per_label_ms",
  format = ms2
)
table <- table[order(table$Content == "Math", table$Labels), ]
knitr::kable(table, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrr")
```

With 10 labels, each label also carries a share of the layer's fixed cost; from 100 labels on,
the cost per label is steady. In the math panels, `ggplot2` draws plotmath
(`geom_text(parse = TRUE)`).

## Annotations

Each `annotate_typst()` call adds one label, so 10 annotations are 10 layers.
`annotate("text")` and `annotate("richtext")` place all 10 labels in one layer.

```{r}
#| label: annotate-table
annotate <- results[results$section == "annotate", ]
annotate$Function <- annotate$method
annotate$Labels <- annotate$n
knitr::kable(
  by_device(annotate, c("Function", "Labels")),
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = "lrrr"
)
```

For more than a few labels, a `geom_*()` layer with a data frame is cheaper than many
`annotate_*()` calls, since every layer has its own overhead.

## Theme elements

Each case draws the plot's text with `element_text()`, `ggtext::element_markdown()`, or
`element_typst()`, set on every element involved:

- **Titles**: title, subtitle, caption, and the two axis titles (5 labels).
- **Axis text**: 10 tick labels on each axis (20 labels).
- **Legend**: a legend title and 8 keys (9 labels).
- **Strips**: 12 facet panels (12 strip labels).
- **All**: all of the above in one faceted plot, where tick labels repeat on every outer panel.

```{r}
#| label: theme-table
theme_results <- results[results$section == "theme", ]
case_names <- c(
  titles = "Titles",
  axis_text = "Axis text",
  legend = "Legend",
  strips = "Strips",
  all = "All"
)
theme_results$Case <- factor(
  case_names[theme_results$content],
  levels = case_names
)
theme_results$Element <- theme_results$method
table <- by_device(theme_results, c("Case", "Element"))
table <- table[order(table$Case), ]
knitr::kable(table, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrr")
```

Titles, legends, and strips cost about the same with `ggtypst` as with `ggtext`. Many tick
labels cost more, especially in PDF: `ggtypst` lays out and draws every tick label on its own, in
every panel where it appears.

## Saving the same plot again

`ggplot2` builds and draws the whole plot again each time it is printed or saved, for example
when the plot pane is resized or when `ggsave()` follows `print()`. These cases save a plot that
was already saved once.

```{r}
#| label: redraw-table
redraw <- results[
  results$section %in%
    c("geom", "theme", "redraw") &
    (results$n %in% 100 | results$content %in% "all") &
    results$method != "geom_point only",
]
redraw$Plot <- ifelse(
  is.na(redraw$n),
  "All theme text",
  sprintf(
    "%d %s labels",
    redraw$n,
    ifelse(redraw$content == "math", "math", "styled")
  )
)
redraw$Function <- redraw$method
redraw$Save <- ifelse(redraw$measure == "second", "Second", "First")
table <- by_device(redraw, c("Plot", "Function", "Save"))
table <- table[order(table$Plot, table$Function, table$Save), ]
knitr::kable(table, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllrr")
```

Saving a plot again takes about as long as saving it the first time, with every package.

## First plot in a new session

Each run starts a new R session, loads `ggplot2` and the package, then builds and saves a plot
with 10 labels. "Load" is the time to load the packages, "First plot" the time to build and save
the plot.

```{r}
#| label: cold-table
cold <- results[results$section == "cold start", ]
cold$Package <- ifelse(cold$package == "ggplot2", "ggplot2 only", cold$package)
cold$Function <- cold$method
cold$Step <- factor(
  c(
    load = "Load",
    "first plot" = "First plot",
    "load and first plot" = "Total"
  )[
    cold$measure
  ],
  levels = c("Load", "First plot", "Total")
)
table <- by_device(cold, c("Package", "Function", "Step"))
table <- table[order(table$Step, table$Package), ]
knitr::kable(table, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllrr")
```

Loading `ggtypst` costs about `r ms(load_time("ggtypst") - load_time("ggplot2"))` more than
`ggplot2` alone. Its first plot takes longer than later ones, because `ggtypst` finds the
installed fonts and starts Typst the first time it renders a label.

## Practical guidelines

1. **Estimate the cost of a label layer** as the time of the plot without labels plus the number
   of labels times the cost per label above, about `r ms2(png_typst)` for PNG and
   `r ms2(pdf_typst)` for PDF on this machine. A plot with `r max_rows` labels takes about
   `r ms(result(section = "geom", method = "geom_typst", device = "png", n = max_rows))` as
   PNG.
2. **Use `geom_text()` for plain text.** When labels need no styling or math, `ggplot2`'s own
   text is the fastest option.
3. **For label layers, `ggtypst` is faster than `ggtext`** at every size measured here, and
   also draws math.
4. **Use one `geom_*()` layer instead of many `annotate_*()` calls** for more than a few labels.
5. **For PDF, consider the device.** `pdf()` draws `ggtypst` text as outlines, which looks the
   same on every computer but is slower to draw. Devices that embed fonts, such as
   `cairo_pdf()`, draw native glyphs instead; see `?ggtypst-options`.

## Reproducing the benchmark

The benchmark script is in the package's source repository. From a clone of the repository,
run:

```bash
Rscript tools/benchmark.R
```
